newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Michelin's profits rise, stock skids.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Michelin's profits rise, stock skids.

text.p: Tyre giant Michelin said on Tuesday its 1996 profit rose five percent to 3.11 billion francs ($545.2 million), but the modest gain masked a jump in earnings before exceptional charges.

The stock fell 6.21 percent, however, because the headline figure was lower than anticipated, exceptional charges were greater than expected, and the outlook for Michelin's main markets was discouraging, analysts said.

Cie Generale des Etablissements Michelin, which vies with Japan's Bridgestone for the top global ranking, said that stripping out exceptional charges of 845 million francs, profits rose 36 percent to 3.96 billion francs last year.
It said the rise reflected a 6.4 percent rise in unit sales to record volumes, lower rubber prices and financial expenses, and favourable currency trends.

Michelin's performance was helped by rapid sales gains in emerging markets, while brisk tyre replacement business in the United States helped offset slow growth in U.S. and European car production and downturns in the truck industry.
Turnover rose to 71.25 billion francs from 66.11 billion.
Operating profit increased 22 percent to 6.96 billion francs, approaching the company's minimum target of 10 percent of sales, Finance Director Eric Bourdais de Charbonniere said.
"That's the minimum if we want to compete with Goodyear and Bridgestone," he told a news conference. The three companies share more than half the global market.

The 1997 results should "confirm the favourable trend of recent years," Bourdais de Charbonniere said. Michelin set up a big cost-cutting programme in 1993, and last year reorganised its businesses for faster response to market shifts.
Its 1996 charges included 1.15 billion francs to cut jobs in Spain and France. Bourdais de Charbonniere said the group needed to trim staff but was moving gradually to avoid shocks.
Michelin also took an unexpected 750 million franc charge to cover its exposure to a private bank, Banque Industrielle et Mobiliere Privee, in which it holds 38 percent.
"That was a bolt from the blue," said one analyst.

A 964 million franc gain generated largely from Michelin's sale of a 2.6 percent stake in carmaker PSA Peugeot Citroen brought down the total charge to 845 million francs, which compares with a 72 million franc gain for 1995.
Including the 1996 exceptionals, net attributable profit came to 2.89 billion francs, compared with 2.80 billion for 1995. The market had been expecting a figure around 3.4 billion.
Michelin's stock closed down 21 francs, or 6.21 percent, at 318.50.
"In what doesn't look to be a fast-running marketplace, there's scope for disappointment in the stock," another analyst said.

Since the start of the year, Michelin shares have gained 17 percent, partly on expectations that the group was moving quickly to reduce debt, which ballooned after the acquisition of U.S.-based Uniroyal-Goodrich seven years ago.

Michelin cut its debt by 3.4 billion francs to 22.8 billion in 1996. Analysts foresee further debt reduction resulting from the redemption of convertible bond issues expected to total five billion francs.
But the ensuing rise in the number of shares "means they'll have to work hard to increase earnings per share," the analyst said.
Michelin said in its earnings statement that it expected its efforts to cut costs, encourage innovation and expand in new markets will help the 1997 results.
The group is studying several possible acquisitions in emerging markets, expected to show the biggest growth in tyre sales in coming years, Bourdais de Charbonniere said.
Michelin said it expected tyre markets to follow the pattern seen last year, when sales grew much faster in emerging markets than in Europe, North America and Japan. ($ = 5.704 French Francs)
